opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's sharpened it considerably, and in some ways it's made the problem more urgent. For years I've argued that any AI system deployed in a high-stakes setting needs a model of its own competence. It should know which inputs it can handle reliably and which ones it can't, so it can abstain, ask for help, or hand off to a human. In the classical supervised learning setting we had some decent tools for this: anomaly detection to notice when an input is out of distribution, calibration methods, conformal prediction to get guarantees on prediction sets, and so on.

Large language models break a lot of the assumptions those tools rely on. First, we often don't know what the training distribution even is. It's essentially the whole web plus whatever fine-tuning data the companies used, so the question "is this query out of distribution?" becomes very hard to pose, let alone answer. Second, the outputs are open-ended text rather than a class label, so it's not obvious what it means for an answer to be "correct," or how to put a confidence on it. And third, these systems are extremely fluent. They produce answers that sound authoritative whether or not there's any real knowledge behind them. That's what people call hallucination, but I think of it as a failure of competence modeling. The system doesn't know what it doesn't know, and it has no mechanism for saying so.

What's interesting is that there is some signal in there. Researchers have found that the token probabilities, or the consistency across multiple sampled answers, or probes on the internal representations, carry information about whether the model is likely to be right. So I don't think it's hopeless. But I'd distinguish between that kind of after-the-fact uncertainty estimate and a genuine competence model, which would let the system say, "This is a question about, say, recent case law in a particular jurisdiction, and I know my knowledge there is thin." That requires some representation of the boundaries of its own knowledge, and current architectures don't really have that.

The other thing LLMs have pushed me toward is thinking about the whole system rather than the model alone. If you build an application by wrapping an LLM with retrieval, tools, and verification steps, then competence becomes a property of that larger system. You can check citations against sources, run generated code, use a formal reasoner for the logical parts. I'm increasingly convinced that's the path to trustworthy systems: modular architectures where different components handle different kinds of knowledge and each one can be checked, rather than one giant monolithic network that we just hope is right. Competence modeling is much more tractable when the pieces have well-defined responsibilities.

r001.rationale: The response says AI systems deployed in high-stakes settings need a model of their competence, but does not extend that claim to every machine learning system or clearly describe a trusted domain.

r002.rationale: It discusses detecting out-of-distribution inputs and knowing when the system cannot handle a query, but does not clearly state that recognizing novelty is a prerequisite for responding appropriately to novelty in an open world.

r003.rationale: It lists supervised-learning techniques and explains why LLMs challenge their assumptions, but does not identify computer vision or explicitly raise whether those techniques transfer to LLM competence modeling.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it's forced me to think much harder about what competence actually means, because the thing I had in mind originally was a fairly clean picture. The idea was that a system should have a model of its own competence: a representation of the region of inputs where it can be trusted, and an ability to detect when it's being asked to operate outside that region. For a classifier trained on a well-defined distribution, that's a reasonably tractable problem. You can build an anomaly detector, you can calibrate your confidence, you can refuse to answer.

With large language models, the notion of "the training distribution" sort of dissolves. These models have been trained on an enormous slice of human text, and they're being asked to do essentially open-ended tasks. So the question "is this input in-distribution?" doesn't have a crisp answer anymore. Almost everything is in-distribution in some weak sense, and almost nothing is in-distribution in the strong sense that would let you give guarantees.

What I've come to believe is that competence for these systems has to be defined at the level of tasks and knowledge, not inputs. The model may be extremely competent at syntax, at style, at the kind of reasoning that appears frequently in text, and simultaneously incompetent at knowing specific facts, especially facts that are rare, recent, or that were only mentioned a handful of times in the training data. And the troubling part is that the surface fluency is the same in both cases. The model doesn't speak less confidently when it's making things up. So the competence boundary is invisible from the outside, and I'd argue it's largely invisible to the model itself.

That's actually why I've been pushing on the idea that we should separate the linguistic competence from the factual knowledge. A language model is a wonderful language model. It's a questionable knowledge base. If we treat it as a reasoning and language engine that retrieves from an external, auditable knowledge source, then at least the competence question becomes partly answerable again: did the retrieval find relevant, trustworthy information or not? That's something you can measure.

The other shift in my thinking is about calibration. In the classic setting, I wanted a probability on each prediction. With these systems, what I really want is something more like the model being able to say "I know this," "I'm inferring this," or "I'm guessing." And we've seen some encouraging work on getting models to express uncertainty, but we've also seen that the standard training pipelines, particularly the reinforcement learning from human feedback step, tend to reward sounding confident. So you can actually train the calibration out of the model. That's a real tension between making a system pleasant to use and making it honest about its competence.

So I'd say the rise of LLMs hasn't made the competence problem go away. If anything, it's made it more urgent and harder, because we now have systems that are deployed to millions of people, that are competent in a huge range of situations, and that fail in ways that look identical to success.

r001.rationale: The response says a system should model its own competence by representing the region of inputs where it can be trusted.

r002.rationale: It discusses detecting when inputs fall outside a competence region, but does not identify recognizing novelty as a prerequisite for responding appropriately to novelty in an open world.

r003.rationale: It contrasts classifiers trained on a defined distribution with LLMs, but does not raise whether supervised computer vision competence techniques transfer to LLMs.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think large language models have made the need for competence models much more apparent. By a competence model, I mean some way of characterizing where a system can be trusted and where it is likely to fail. And with language models, that boundary is remarkably hard to describe. You can see a system give a very sophisticated answer to one question and then fail on another question that appears much simpler.

So we have to distinguish the ability to produce a plausible answer from the ability to assess whether that answer is correct. Asking the model, “Are you sure?” doesn’t necessarily give us an independent assessment of its competence. It may just produce another plausible piece of text.

That pushes my thinking toward competence assessment at the level of the whole system. Can we check the answer with a tool? Can we identify conditions under which performance deteriorates? Can the system recognize when it needs additional information or should defer to a person? The goal is to make those decisions based on evidence about reliability, rather than the fluency of the response.

r001.rationale: The response says competence models characterize where a system can be trusted, but does not assert that every machine learning system should have a model of its trusted domain.

r002.rationale: The response discusses recognizing limits and when to defer, but does not identify recognizing a novel situation as a prerequisite for responding appropriately to novelty in an open world.

r003.rationale: The response does not raise whether supervised computer vision competence-modeling techniques can transfer to large language models.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, large language models have made me think that we need a much richer notion of competence than a score on a benchmark. A single system can perform an astonishing range of tasks, but its performance can also be very uneven. It may give a good answer to a difficult question and then fail on something that seems much simpler. So we can’t infer from its fluency that it has mastered the underlying task.

A competence model should help us understand under what circumstances we can rely on the system. What kinds of questions can it answer? What information needs to be available? How sensitive is it to the way the problem is presented? And can we recognize when we’ve moved outside those conditions?

There’s also a distinction between producing an answer and assessing whether that answer is correct. Asking the language model whether it’s confident doesn’t, by itself, solve that problem. We need ways to check its work, whether through external tools, independent evidence, or interaction with a person.

So I think the large language models make the need for competence models more pressing. The challenge is to turn this very broad but uneven capability into a system that knows when to proceed, when to seek more information, and when to hand the task back to a human.

r001.rationale: The response says competence models should identify when a system can be relied on, but does not assert that every machine learning system should have a model of its trusted domain.

r002.rationale: It mentions recognizing when conditions have been exceeded, but does not identify recognizing novelty as a prerequisite for responding to novelty in an open world.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss whether supervised computer vision competence techniques transfer to large language models.
